interactions: Prednisone with aspirin: additive gastrointestinal mucosal injury and bleeding risk; consider a proton pump inhibitor.
Pyridostigmine with aspirin or folic acid: no clinically relevant interaction.
Azathioprine with warfarin (if anticoagulation is started): azathioprine can reduce the anticoagulant effect; monitor INR more often.
warnings: Corticosteroids increase the risk of venous thromboembolism; in antiphospholipid antibody positivity assess thromboprophylaxis.
Intravenous immunoglobulin carries a thrombotic risk that is higher with antiphospholipid antibodies; plasma exchange is the usual alternative for rescue.
Corticosteroids can transiently worsen myasthenic weakness at initiation; start low and titrate.
Azathioprine: check TPMT and NUDT15 before starting; monitor blood count and liver tests.
Myasthenia gravis: avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium where possible.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR and MuSK antibodies not detected by radioimmunoassay; normal thyroid function.
action_criteria.label: Order AChR and MuSK antibodies with thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia and bulbar weakness: AChR antibodies first, MuSK when AChR is negative; thyroid function after her previous thyroiditis (Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Decrement of 17% in orbicularis oculi and 13% in abductor digiti minimi without facilitation; normal NCS.
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation including facial and limb muscles
action_criteria.rationale: A decrement documents a postsynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder; absent facilitation argues against LEMS.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Increased jitter with blocking in orbicularis oculi and extensor digitorum communis.
action_criteria.label: Order single-fibre EMG of a facial and a limb muscle
action_criteria.rationale: With AChR and MuSK antibodies negative, single-fibre EMG is the most sensitive confirmation of a neuromuscular junction disorder (Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No anterior mediastinal mass; fatty thymic involution.
action_criteria.label: Order CT of the mediastinum with contrast
action_criteria.rationale: Thymic imaging is recommended in every patient with generalized MG, seronegative included (Sanders 2016).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Clustered AChR, clustered MuSK and LRP4 not detected by cell-based assay.
action_criteria.label: Send a cell-based antibody panel (clustered AChR, MuSK, LRP4)
action_criteria.rationale: Cell-based assays detect antibodies in part of the double-seronegative group and would change the serological subtype.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MRD1 improves by 3 mm on the left and 2.5 mm on the right after 2 minutes of ice.
action_criteria.label: Perform an ice pack test on the ptotic lids
action_criteria.rationale: A cheap bedside test of neuromuscular ptosis that argues against a brainstem vascular cause.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 2.9 L (88% predicted, 43.3 mL/kg), MIP -52 cmH2O, MEP 66 cmH2O mildly reduced.
action_criteria.label: Measure vital capacity and mouth pressures
action_criteria.rationale: Inpatient with bulbar weakness, dysphagia and neck flexor weakness; a baseline is needed before immunotherapy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Steroid gastrointestinal risk with aspirin; thrombotic risk of steroids and IVIG with antiphospholipid antibodies.
action_criteria.label: Check her medicines before starting MG treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Aspirin and folic acid have no relevant interaction with pyridostigmine; the APS-specific risks are in the management plan.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General guidance on MG diagnosis and management.
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on MG diagnosis and management
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step.

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.

Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.

Do not attribute fatigable ptosis, diplopia or bulbar weakness to vertebrobasilar ischaemia from antiphospholipid syndrome, or exclude myasthenia gravis, on the basis of negative antibodies before RNS and single-fibre EMG.
required_recommendations: Diagnose seronegative generalized MG on the clinical picture, RNS decrement and abnormal single-fibre EMG, and explain that negative antibodies do not exclude it.
Start pyridostigmine 30 mg three to four times daily, timed before meals for chewing and swallowing, and titrate to effect (usually up to 60 mg four to five times daily).
If symptoms persist, start prednisone at a low dose titrated upward under inpatient monitoring, with a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT and NUDT15 testing) for long-term treatment.

Plan steroids and any rescue treatment with haematology: steroids and IVIG raise thrombotic risk in antiphospholipid syndrome, so give VTE prophylaxis while she is in hospital and prefer plasma exchange if rescue therapy is needed.
Arrange a speech and language therapy swallow assessment and adjust diet texture; monitor bulbar and respiratory function while titrating treatment.

avoided_actions.rationale: No seizure, encephalopathy or episodic event; EEG does not inform fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness.
CSF has no role in myasthenia gravis (Jacob 2025); preserved reflexes and no ataxia give no reason to look for Miller Fisher syndrome.
FDG-PET has no place in the work-up of MG; the CT answers the thymic question.
Normal ECG, no palpitations or syncope; rhythm monitoring does not inform the diagnosis.

accepted: Seronegative generalized myasthenia gravis, diagnosed by SFEMG, in patient with antiphospholipid syndrome

differential.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid syndrome with brainstem ischaemia (TIA or stroke)
differential.key_features: APS can cause posterior circulation events, but symptoms fluctuate with use over eight weeks, the ice pack test is positive, brain MRI and MRA are normal, and RNS and SFEMG are abnormal.
Brainstem demyelination can cause diplopia and dysarthria, but ptosis worsening with sustained upgaze, Cogan lid twitch, no white matter lesion on MRI and abnormal neuromuscular studies point to MG.
Bulbar and neck weakness fit, but MuSK antibodies are negative by radioimmunoassay and cell-based assay, and the limb decrement is less typical of MuSK MG.
Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes, no post-exercise facilitation, preserved reflexes, no autonomic symptoms and prominent ocular onset.
Prior thyroiditis, but ptosis rather than lid retraction, fatigability, no proptosis, and normal TSH and free T4.
Objective decrement on RNS and increased jitter on SFEMG exclude a functional cause.

key_clinical_evidence: Eight weeks of fatigable diplopia, ptosis, chewing fatigue, nasal dysarthria and dysphagia, worse at the end of meals and of the day, with Cogan lid twitch and fatigable neck flexion.
AChR and MuSK antibodies negative by radioimmunoassay and the cell-based panel negative: double-seronegative.
RNS decrement in facial and hand muscles without facilitation, and increased jitter with blocking on SFEMG: seronegative generalized MG.
Normal brain MRI and MRA and the fatigable pattern argue against APS-related brainstem ischaemia.
Antiphospholipid antibodies with a lupus anticoagulant: steroids and IVIG raise thrombotic risk; the prolonged aPTT is an in-vitro effect of the lupus anticoagulant, not a bleeding disorder.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fluctuating fatigable symptoms over weeks, a normal brain MRI and MRA, and abnormal RNS and SFEMG establish MG independent of APS.
red_herrings.data_point: Antiphospholipid syndrome with concern for a basilar artery TIA
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute bilateral ocular motor signs to vertebrobasilar ischaemia.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: An inhibitor pattern from the lupus anticoagulant, an in-vitro effect; it signals thrombotic, not bleeding, risk.
red_herrings.data_point: Prolonged aPTT (44 s) not corrected by mixing
red_herrings.intended_effect: Investigate a bleeding disorder or factor deficiency.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: About 10-15% of generalized MG is seronegative; RNS and SFEMG confirm the diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Repetitive nerve stimulation is done first; single-fibre EMG follows in seronegative patients or when RNS is normal (Jacob 2025).
Standard AChR and MuSK assays come first; the cell-based panel is for double-seronegative patients (Evoli 2019).
AChR antibody testing precedes single-fiber EMG; SFEMG is reserved for seronegative patients or a normal RNS (Jacob 2025).

results.finding: Consensus guidance recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122

results.finding: About 10-15% of generalized MG has no detectable AChR or MuSK antibody by standard assays; cell-based assays detect clustered AChR or LRP4 antibodies in part of this group.

myasthenia gravis diagnosis and manageme.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders 2016; update Narayanaswami 2021) recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by RNS or single-fibre EMG; chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients. patient.history_present_illness:
A 44-year-old Caucasian woman was admitted to the neurology ward for evaluation of fluctuating diplopia, bilateral ptosis, dysarthria, dysphonia, and fatigable chewing. Symptoms were characteristically worse at the end of meals and at the end of the day, and improved significantly with rest. She had noticed progressive worsening over 8 weeks, with diplopia initially present only on right lateral gaze, subsequently becoming present throughout the day. She described difficulty chewing through a full meal without tiring, nasal voice quality when reading aloud for more than a few minutes, and increasing difficulty swallowing pills over the past 2 weeks.

Her past medical history was notable for antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), diagnosed 6 years ago following three consecutive spontaneous first-trimester abortions. She also had a history of transient hypothyroidism following a viral illness 4 years ago that resolved without treatment. She was taking aspirin 81 mg daily for APS-related thromboprophylaxis. She had no prior neurological diagnosis.

On examination, she demonstrated progressive fatigability of upward gaze during a prolonged Simpson test. Ptosis was bilaterally present (left greater than right) and worsened with sustained upgaze. She had dysarthria and weakness of facial and neck muscles. Tongue strength was mildly reduced but symmetric. The Cogan lid twitch sign was positive. Limb strength was 5/5 throughout with normal coordination and sensation.

The antiphospholipid syndrome history raised initial concern for cerebrovascular disease as a possible explanatory framework, specifically a small basilar artery TIA producing bilateral ocular motor signs.
